title: Bramble's Lost Dewdrop Rescue
markdown:
The Sunspike Peaks were a place of wind and wonder. The wind did not merely blow; it whispered and tickled the nose with wild thyme. Sunbeams danced like tiny golden sprites on the green hills.

On this morning Bramble the witch was in a tizzy. Hair the colour of moonlight spun fine puffed up like dandelion fluff. Her favourite shimmering dewdrop—the one she had found in a spider’s web, catching the dawn like a tiny star—was gone. Vanished. Without its glow, her Sparkle Bloom potion for the Sunspike Market would have no dazzling sparkle, and Bramble would be quite disappointed.

Her button nose twitched. “Oh dear, oh dear.” A fluttery tickly feeling in her tummy made her knees feel like wobbly jelly. She wished she could hide under her quilt until breakfast.

Corvus the raven perched on the windowsill, eyes like shiny black beads. Clever, and a bit of a busybody. He hopped down with a soft flap. “Caw. A clue.” He pecked at something tiny and almost invisible on Bramble’s spellbook. A silvery thread.

“That is from the Elf Weaver’s cloak.” The Elf Weaver lived deep in the Whispering Woods.

She grabbed her leather satchel, the one with embroidered stars, and slung it over her shoulder. Corvus puffed out his chest, wings twitching. With the wind nudging them like a friend, they set off.

The Whispering Woods were a place where the trees really did whisper. Leaves rustled secrets. The air hummed. Under the leafy roof the light turned soft and green. A small figure darted from behind an old mossy oak: Pipkin, an elf guide, tunic the colour of fresh moss, smile as bright as a sunbeam.

“A witch and her raven.” His voice like the tinkle of tiny silver bells. “The market opens soon, and your Sparkle Bloom is almost as popular as my grandmother’s wild berry pies.” He winked, as if he already knew why she had come.

Corvus was not listening. He was sure Bramble had simply misplaced the dewdrop somewhere silly, tucked it into a pocket and forgotten. “Caw. Silly witch.” With a determined flap he dived into a patch of ferns, certain he would find it sparkling on a ladybug’s back. Bramble watched him go. A small sigh. Her grandmother, a wise witch with laughter lines, had once said the greatest magic was not always in the spell you cast.

Corvus’s hunt caused quite a commotion. He thought he saw a sparkle. He swooped low, flapped high, and in his zeal flew right past Bramble’s satchel. A cloud of the most delicate silvery moon-moth dust—collected over many nights, needed so the potion’s shimmer would catch the light just so—flew everywhere. Scattered like a million tiny diamonds.

“Corvus.” Dismay. The fluttery feeling returned, stronger. Her dearest friend, with his best intentions, had made things worse. She squeezed her eyes shut. The woods went quiet. Damp earth. Ancient trees. A gentle breeze in her hair. She took a breath and felt the stillness.

Pipkin had been watching with a gentle amused smile. “Corvus, you certainly are a whirlwind.” Bramble looked at her raven, who now looked a little sheepish. She looked at the scattered dust, then at Pipkin brushing a speck from a fern leaf. Corvus was not being a bother. He was worried about her. He just did not know how to show it without making a fuss.

A prickle of annoyance rose. She wanted to scold. Instead she took another breath.

“Corvus, the dewdrop is important, yes, but it is not lost forever. And the moon-moth dust is all right. We can gather it again.” She knelt and reached out a hand. “You are worried about me, aren’t you?” He blinked his shiny dark eyes and, with a soft coo, nudged her hand with his beak.

Ravens are much cleverer than they look. Corvus suddenly let out a loud insistent caw and pointed his beak toward Pipkin’s satchel, open on the moss. Pipkin peered inside. Tangled in a particularly fuzzy bit of his woven cloak, glinting with a captured sunbeam, was Bramble’s shimmering dewdrop.

“My goodness gracious. How on earth did that get there?”

“He found it.” A wide joyous smile. Corvus puffed out his chest, preening. Bramble carefully unhooked the dewdrop. Pipkin gently retrieved his cloak. Corvus, with a triumphant caw that echoed through the trees, watched over them both.

Then a small anxious chirp from Pipkin. “Oh dear. I promised my little sister I would bring her some of my special sparkle berries from the top of the Sunspike Peaks. I have been so busy I completely forgot.” He looked so sad. Bramble knew how important promises were. She looked at her potion, still bubbling gently. She looked at the tiny sparkle berries that had spilled from Pipkin’s pouch near his feet. Then, with a careful scoop, she took a small handful of her own precious moon-moth dust—the bits that had not scattered too far—and sprinkled it over the spilled berries. “These will be extra sparkly now. A special gift from all of us.” Pipkin’s face lit up.

They hurried back to Bramble’s cottage, the wind whispering cheerful encouragement, the trees rustling as if they were singing. Bramble poured the dewdrop into her cauldron, then the sparkling berries, then the gathered moon-moth dust. With a little gentle coaxing the dust swirled in. The Sparkle Bloom shimmered even more beautifully than usual, with a radiant glow.

As the colourful market stalls opened, banners fluttering, Bramble, Pipkin, and Corvus stood side by side. Customers admired the potion. Corvus perched proudly on her shoulder, a sleek ebony guardian. Pipkin offered them both a slice of his famous wild berry pie, and a handful of the super-sparkly berries for Bramble’s own enjoyment. The market smelled of thyme and warm pastry. The dewdrop, safe in the cauldron, kept shining.
characters: Bramble (young witch who brews Sparkle Bloom), Corvus (a raven who pecks at clues)
author: StoryGen Community
